sources.news_title: Illinois medical debt relief program surpasses $1B goal in two years
Illinois taxpayers foot $10M bill to forgive $1.4B in medical debt - Regional Media News
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – Cook County and state of Illinois officials gathered Thursday to announce roughly $1.4 billion in medical debt has been cancelled through both a state and local program for Illinois residents, but studies show that such programs may not always be beneficial.
Illinois taxpayers footed the $10 million bill to cancel the debt of about 694,000 residents, with the program costing pennies on the dollar for the state to purchase medical debt that is either about to or already has been sent to a collection agency.
Gov. J.B. Pritzker, who proposed the statewide program based on Cook County’s two years ago, celebrated the erasing of debt by the state.
“The average recipient had nearly $1,600 of debt canceled. One Illinoisan received $900,000 in relief. In 40 different Illinois counties, more than 5% of residents received relief from this program,” Pritzker said. “For example, nearly 22% of residents living in Kankakee County have benefited from this program.”
Pritzker also explained why he feels the program is impactful for the residents who have received a letter notifying them of their cancelled debt.
“Medical debt is a leading cause of bankruptcy. It impacts people’s ability to pay rent, their ability to put food on the table, or just to save for the future. It can ruin credit, limit financial opportunities, and cause years of uncertainty long after they leave the hospital,” Pritzker said.
But some research suggests the cancellation of medical debt may not be as impactful to assisting recipients financially.
Lead author on a 2024 National Bureau of Economic Research report, Neale Mahoney, said in a subsequent article explaining the interpretation of the study’s findings that most recipients of medical debt relief the study surveyed didn’t see an impact to their credit rating after debt was cancelled.
Mahoney attributed the general lack of impact to a “shift in the credit reporting environment,” as a lot of medical debt has stopped being reported to credit agencies in the first place.
He suggested programs like Illinois’ choose to specifically target people with debt that is impacting their credit first to have a stronger impact.
The study also found lackluster results in improving recipient’s payment of other existing medical bills.
The state program is conducted in partnership with the nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, which assists the state in finding and buying the medical debt of residents. Mahoney’s study was conducted with the nonprofit.
Em Brostek, a public relations manager for Undue Medical Debt, said the company’s approach was informed by the study and has since been adjusted to expand eligibility to anyone at 400% of the federal poverty level and providing relief recipients with other resources upstream of having other medical bills go unpaid.
Pritzker told reporters after the announcement that he wants the state to continue to find funds for the program, even as budgeting with the available state taxpayer funds becomes more difficult each year.
“I don’t know any other program that has that kind of return for people. So, it’s one that I really believe in. I mean, we’re going to have to work hard to find those dollars,” Pritzker said. “I’m hopeful that as we continue to identify debt that we can relieve, that we’ll be able to find the dollars in our state budget.”

sources.news_title: Illinois erases $1.4 billion in medical debt for thousands of residents - IPM Newsroom
sources.text:
A statewide effort has so far eliminated more than $1.4 billion in medical debt for thousands of Illinois residents, Gov. JB Pritzker announced Thursday at a news conference.
Pritzker touted the results of the state’s Medical Debt Relief Program, which started about two years ago. The state had allocated $10 million toward the program, and Pritzker said in the Cook County Health building that he’s committed to continuing funding for the program.
“One of the great things about this program is that the return on investment is so high,” Pritzker said. “Every penny that we put in relieves a dollar of debt. I don’t know any other program that has that kind of return for people.”
Pritzker said the program aims to address the unaffordable financial burden residents are saddled with because of an unexpected injury or illness. The state program has reached 694,000 residents, according to Pritzker’s office. On average, residents had about $1,200 in debt eliminated, though one person had as much as $900,000 in medical debt erased, according to the state.
Pritzker was joined by Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle who first implemented a medical debt relief program in the county. The state and county programs combined have eliminated $2.4 billion in debt for about 1.5 million residents, according to the state and county officials.
Cook County used federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act to start the local program, but Preckwinkle also said she’s committed to continue funding the initiative once those federal funds end.
“The next phase of this work will put data from this initiative to use to understand who is being pushed into medical debt and why, and to design policies that address its root causes,” Preckwinkle said.
The state and county have worked with Undue Medical Debt, a nonprofit that negotiates the sale or donation of portfolios of medical debt with hospitals and health systems. Eligible households typically have to have an income at or below 400% of the federal poverty level.
The program stands out from others in that residents do not apply for it. Instead, a person who’s had their medical debt eliminated by the state or county programs receives a letter in the mail notifying them of how much debt was erased, Pritzker said.
“I’ve talked to some folks who’ve received a letter like that; people have broken out crying,” Pritzker said. “People want to pay their debts. They do, and they get bills in the mail that they know they are obligated, that they’re supposed to pay, and with medical debt, they often just can’t — it’s too much.”
In suburban DuPage County, about 7% of residents had debt erased by the state’s program. Nearly 13% of Kane County residents had medical debt eliminated, along with nearly 9% of residents in Lake County. About 22% of residents in Kankakee County, about 60 miles south of Chicago, had their medical debt eliminated as well.

sources.news_title: Cook County medical debt relief program expands to Illinois
sources.text:
Over $1.4B in medical debt has been erased for nearly 700K Illinoisans across all counties
CHICAGO (WLS) -- The state has erased over $1.4 billion in medical debt for almost 700,000 Illinoisans for pennies on the dollar, two years after launching a new relief program.
At its launch, the Illinois Medical Debt Relief Program aimed to eliminate $1 billion in debt. The state has surpassed that goal by $400 million, spending less than $10 million in state dollars to achieve these results. That means that every state dollar invested in the program wiped out over $100 in debt.
That was possible due to the state's partnership with Undue Medical Debt — a nonprofit that works with local governments and healthcare providers to purchase and eliminate qualifying medical debt owed by low-income residents.
"Medical debt is a leading cause of bankruptcy," Gov. JB Pritzker said in a news conference Thursday in Chicago. "It can ruin credit, limit financial opportunities, and cause years of uncertainty long after they leave the hospital. That is a symptom of a truly broken system."
Illinois residents whose household income is at or below 400% of the federal poverty level, or who have medical debt equal to 5% or more of their household income, are eligible.
Residents do not apply to this program — impacted households receive letters after their debts have been erased.
READ ALSO | Since 2022, Cook County has erased over $1B in medical debt for more than 791K residents
"Healthcare should be about getting people back on their feet, not just keeping them, well, down with years of financial struggle," Pritzker said.
The statewide initiative was modeled after Cook County's program that launched in 2022. Since then, the Cook County Medical Debt Relief Initiative has eliminated an additional $1 billion in medical debt, covering 22% of eligible adults.
The American Rescue Plan Act funded the Cook County initiative to support recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. These funds end this year, Toni Preckwinkle, president of the Cook County Board of Commissioners, said.
"At a time when the Trump administration is stepping back from its federal responsibility to working families, Cook County and the state of Illinois are standing firm in our belief that access to quality healthcare should not depend on your income or your ability to pay," Preckwinkle said.
Recently, President Donald Trump and the federal government have rolled out cuts to Medicaid, a program that provides free or low-cost coverage to people with limited income and resources.
The Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services warned that two policy changes are expected by the beginning of 2027 and may reduce Illinoisans' eligibility: redeterminations every six months for Medicare eligibility instead of every year and a federal work requirement.
For Steph Willding, CEO of Community Health, a center offering free services for low-income, uninsured and underinsured patients, access to healthcare should never be connected to their ability to pay.
"We know the value of taking away the barrier of cost for our patients, and as federal policy changes continue to threaten healthcare coverage for more and more Illinoisans, this program has never been more important," said Willding at a news conference.
The average debt relieved of the medical debt relief program per resident was over $1,200, while the highest amount eliminated was over $900,000.
The program relieved debt for residents in all 102 Illinois counties. In 40 counties, more than 5% of residents received debt relief. In 11 counties with populations over 100,000, the percentage was even higher, with Kankakee County at over 21.5%.
Although Cook County will fund this initiative from its own budget, Preckwinkle said they aren't willing to walk away from the program.
"The next phase of this work will put data from this initiative to use to understand who is being pushed into medical debt and why, and to design policies that address its root causes," Preckwinkle said.
Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service covering state government. It is distributed to hundreds of print and broadcast outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation, along with major contributions from the Illinois Broadcasters Foundation and Southern Illinois Editorial Association.
Visit arpa.cookcountyil.gov/medical-debt-relief-initiative for more information.

Illinois erases $1.4 billion in medical debt for 700,000 citizens
Illinois wipes out $1.4B in medical debt for residents
‘Who Pays the Debt?’: Critics Question Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker’s $1.4 Billion Medical Debt Relief for Nearly 700,000 Residents
sources.text:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker posted on X that the state has erased $1.4 billion in medical debt for nearly 700,000 residents. The announcement described the relief as helping people avoid years of financial struggle and included a video of the governor speaking about the program. Online users responded by questioning who ultimately covers the cost, with many comments stating that Illinois taxpayers are paying for the debt cancellation.
The video shows Pritzker at a podium discussing letters sent to residents under the program. In the clip, he says, “I’ve talked to some of the folks who’ve received a letter like that; people have broken out crying,” and adds that recipients “want to pay their debts” but “with medical debt they often just can’t, it’s too much.”
He describes the automatic relief as meaningful for public service because of its “direct impact on so many people.”
According to the post and related official statements, the Illinois Medical Debt Relief Program has erased more than $1.4 billion in debt for nearly 700,000 residents across all 102 counties, exceeding an initial $1 billion goal while using less than $10 million in state funds.
The state works with the nonprofit Undue Medical Debt to buy unpaid medical bills at a big discount and cancel them for low-income residents. No one has to apply. On average, people got about $1,200 wiped out, and one person had as much as $900,000 canceled.
Responses to the Illinois Medical Debt Relief Announcement
Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle backed the program. She said she was glad the state built on what the county had already done and called medical debt relief “one of the most effective investments government can make.”
State senators Lakesia Collins and Mike Simmons also spoke in support. Collins said, “Behind every one of those 700,000 people is a family that can finally breathe again,” and called the program a real difference for communities.
Simmons said the goal was simple, “no one should lose their financial footing because they got sick”, and pointed to the $1.4 billion erased as proof it worked.
On X, many commenters questioned the funding and described the relief as a cost shifted to taxpayers. One wrote, “You can’t just ‘forgive’ debt that isn’t yours to forgive. So in fact, the lawful citizens of Illinois are paying off that debt under your supervision.”
Another said, “Who pays the debt? That’s right. You take money from people who didn’t accrue the debt.”
A third added, “Again, Illinois taxpayers foot the bill for another worthless program.”
Discussion of the medical debt program has continued online and among state officials. Supporters point to the number of Illinois residents who received relief, while critics keep returning to the question of taxpayer funding.
